# 2. For each bit position, compute the CRC difference (remainder)
# 3. Set up GF(2) linear system: CRC(x) XOR x = 0
# 4. Solve with Gaussian elimination over GF(2)

# Rows represent the CRC output bits XOR input bits

# Giant step: check if a * g^(-x2) is in baby table

# setcontext loads registers from offsets relative to RDX (which points to fp->_wide_data):
#   RSP from [rdx+0xa0], RIP from [rdx+0xa8], RDI from [rdx+0x68]
## House of Einherjar — Off-by-One Null Byte (0xFun 2026)
# Fake chunk layout (at known heap address fake_addr):
#     size:           target_size | PREV_INUSE  (must match consolidation math)
#     fd_nextsize:    fake_addr   (self-referencing, needed for large chunks)
# Victim chunk's prev_size must equal distance from fake_chunk to victim
# Off-by-one NUL clears victim's PREV_INUSE bit
# free(victim) triggers backward consolidation: merges with fake_chunk
# Result: consolidated chunk overlaps other live allocations
# Example: Codegate 2013 Vuln 400 — board-based heap grooming
# Step 1: Create 7 posts with overflow in content field
# Step 2: Fill reply buffers to heap-spray "sh" strings
# Step 3: Delete 5 of 7 to create specific heap holes
# Step 4: Allocate 2 new entries into freed space
# Step 5: Trigger via modify + delete sequence

# Next alloc returns target_addr — use to overwrite atexit handlers

# Size must be < MINSIZE away from page boundary
# Step 2: Request larger than corrupted top size
# Forces sysmalloc → old top freed into unsorted bin

# Forge fake fastbin chunk on the stack

# Step 2: Forge fake chunk in target area
# fake->fd must point back to the real smallbin chunk
# fake->bk must point to another valid-looking chunk (or same)
# Step 3: Overwrite chunk_a->bk to point to our fake chunk
# Step 4: Two allocations from this smallbin

headings: # Universal (fat) binaries — multiple architectures in one file
# objc_msgSend(receiver, selector, ...) is THE dispatch mechanism
# RDI = self (receiver), RSI = selector (char* method name)
# Swift uses value witness tables (VWT) for type operations
# Protocol witness tables (PWT) for dynamic dispatch (like vtables)
# Small strings (≤15 bytes): inline in 16-byte buffer, tagged pointer
# Large strings: heap-allocated, pointer + length + flags
# Dictionary<K,V>: hash table with open addressing
# Check if encrypted (App Store encryption / FairPlay DRM)
# Or use Clutch / bfdecrypt on device
# DYLD environment variables (for analysis, blocked in hardened runtime)
# Note: SIP (System Integrity Protection) blocks this for system binaries
# Inspect dyld shared cache (contains all system frameworks)
# If custom compression: try different compressors (-comp xz|lzma|lzo|gzip)
# Extract vmlinux from compressed: vmlinux-to-elf tool
# ARM vs Thumb: ARM instructions are 4 bytes, Thumb are 2 bytes
# LSB of function pointer indicates mode: 0=ARM, 1=Thumb
# Ghidra: Right-click → Processor Options → ARM/Thumb mode
# Big-endian vs little-endian — check ELF header or file command
# Branch delay slots — instruction AFTER branch always executes
# $gp (global pointer) — used for PIC, points to .got
# lui + addiu pair — loads 32-bit constant (upper 16 + lower 16)
# Key pattern: .unlocked_ioctl = my_ioctl_handler in file_operations struct
# In Ghidra: find struct with function pointers, identify by position
# Look for init_module / cleanup_module entry points
# Dump eBPF programs from running system
# r0 = return value, r1-r5 = arguments, r10 = frame pointer
# .sys files are PE format — load in IDA/Ghidra as normal PE
# ObReferenceObjectByHandle → get kernel object from handle
# Reflection system — UCLASS(), UPROPERTY(), UFUNCTION() macros
# In Ghidra: look for UClass::StaticClass() calls → type identification
# String handling: FString (UTF-16), FName (hashed identifier), FText (localized)
# In memory: FString = {TCHAR* Data, int32 ArrayNum, int32 ArrayMax}
# AssetStudio — extract textures, models, audio, scripts
# UABE (Unity Asset Bundle Extractor) — low-level asset editing
# Many games embed Lua for scripting
# Look for: lua51.dll, luajit.dll, .lua files in assets
# Hook lua_pcall to intercept script execution

## Ruby Regexp.escape Multibyte Character Bypass (Square CTF 2017)
# Regexp.escape escapes special chars by prepending backslash
# Vulnerability: byte 0xBF followed by 0x5C (backslash) is a valid GBK character
# Regexp.escape sees 0xBF → not a special char, passes through
# Then sees 0x5C → escapes it to 0x5C 0x5C (double backslash)
# But in GBK: 0xBF 0x5C is ONE character (the lead byte absorbs the backslash)
# The second backslash then escapes the NEXT character, not the intended one
# Result: subsequent input characters become unescaped in the regex
# In a CTF context: HTTP request with GBK lead byte in parameter
# %bf%5c in URL-encoded form — in GBK this is one character
# When Ruby calls Regexp.escape on the input, the backslash is consumed
# If backend uses: /#{Regexp.escape(params[:q])}/  as a regex pattern
# The .* passes through unescaped, matching any string
# In GBK context: first two bytes are one char, leaving ".*" unescaped
# Pattern becomes: /\xbf\\.*/ which in GBK matches the flag (greedy .*)
# Bypass /proc filter to read environment variables
